sections.section_title: Atypical Neck Swelling: Presentation and Initial Clinical Priorities
sections.description: Frames the patient’s subacute neck oedema and early decision-making, emphasizing airway/infection triage, reasons angioedema was suspected, and bedside clues that pointed toward an inflammatory myopathy rather than true angioedema.
subtopics: Presenting features: progressive cervical soft-tissue swelling, mild myalgia, proximal hip-flexor weakness; stable vitals without sepsis
Airway- and infection-first approach to neck swelling: ruling out Ludwig’s angina and deep neck space infection; role of CT neck and urgent ENT nasendoscopy

Why angioedema was suspected and why it was atypical: absence of drug triggers/family history, lack of urticaria, non-tender non-pitting swelling, poor fit with histaminergic or bradykinin-mediated patterns

Examination clues to dermatomyositis: facial erythema (including nasolabial folds), periungual telangiectasias/microhaemorrhages on nailfold capillaroscopy, subtle proximal weakness, thigh rash (Holster sign)
Early laboratory context: modest inflammatory markers without infectious source; prompting a creatine kinase (CK) to evaluate for occult myositis

sections.section_title: From Suspected Angioedema to Autoimmune Myopathy: Diagnostic Workup and Reasoning
sections.description: Details the stepwise investigations, how each data point shifted probability away from angioedema and infection toward dermatomyositis, and how the final diagnosis of anti-SAE1–positive dermatomyositis was established.
subtopics: Trigger to pivot workup: markedly elevated CK (≈16,000 U/L) and interpretation of AST/ALT/LDH as myocyte rather than hepatic injury
Angioedema evaluation: normal C4 and C1-esterase inhibitor quantity/function arguing against hereditary/acquired bradykinin-mediated angioedema
Myositis imaging: MRI thighs showing muscle oedema; FDG-PET mapping diffuse active myositis and serving as malignancy screen

Swallowing and respiratory assessment: videofluoroscopic evidence of severe pharyngeal dysphagia; extrathoracic restrictive pattern on PFTs; chest CT features consistent with aspiration rather than interstitial lung disease
Autoantibody testing: high-titre speckled ANA; strongly positive anti-SAE1 on myositis panel with other MSAs negative (Mi-2, TIF1-γ, Jo-1, OJ)
Muscle biopsy hallmarks of dermatomyositis: perifascicular necrosis/regeneration, perimysial inflammation, and capillary C5b-9 (MAC) deposition

Integrative diagnostic reasoning: why dermatomyositis best fits over immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (anti-HMGCR/SRP; diffuse necrosis, fewer cutaneous signs), inclusion body myositis (older age, distal/finger flexor weakness, rimmed vacuoles), myasthenia gravis (fatigability, ocular signs, normal CK), and infectious/dermatologic mimics (cellulitis/erysipelas, DRESS, urticarial vasculitis, SVC syndrome)

sections.section_title: Dermatomyositis Pathobiology with Emphasis on SAE1-Positive Phenotype and Pseudoangioedema
sections.description: Provides targeted background needed to understand this presentation: the immune microangiopathy of dermatomyositis, why strap/oropharyngeal muscle involvement can mimic angioedema, and the clinical phenotype associated with anti-SAE1 antibodies, including malignancy risk.
subtopics: Immune microangiopathy in dermatomyositis: complement-mediated (C5b-9) capillary injury, perifascicular ischaemia, and the type I interferon signature
Mechanisms of soft-tissue oedema in dermatomyositis vs true angioedema: inflammatory vascular leak and lymphatic congestion from myositis rather than mast cell or bradykinin pathways
Oropharyngeal and strap muscle involvement: pathophysiology of dysphagia, aspiration risk, and extrathoracic restrictive physiology
Anti-SAE1 biology (sumoylation pathway) and clinical associations: prominent cutaneous disease, high rates of dysphagia and interstitial lung disease, and reported malignancy frequency
Epidemiology of ‘pseudoangioedema’ in dermatomyositis and why neck-dominant swelling is uncommon yet clinically important

sections.section_title: Management of Severe Dermatomyositis with Airway and Swallow Involvement
sections.description: Explains the therapeutic strategy used in this case and general principles for treating severe dermatomyositis with dysphagia/airway risk, including induction, steroid-sparing therapy, IVIG, infection prevention, and monitoring.
subtopics: Acute stabilization and supportive care: airway vigilance with ENT, aspiration precautions, nutrition via nasogastric tube, and early speech-language pathology involvement
Glucocorticoid induction: IV methylprednisolone pulses followed by an oral prednisone taper—goals, monitoring CK/strength, and taper strategy
Steroid-sparing immunomodulators: rationale, dosing, and monitoring for mycophenolate mofetil; role of rituximab in severe or refractory disease
Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG): indications in dysphagia-predominant or severe dermatomyositis and typical loading/maintenance schedules
Agents deferred and why: avoiding methotrexate given abnormal lung function/ILD risk; reserving azathioprine or tacrolimus when MMF is effective/tolerated
Infection prevention: PJP prophylaxis choices (TMP-SMX vs nebulized pentamidine when intolerance occurs), baseline viral/hepatitis/TB screening, vaccination timing in immunosuppressed patients
Assessing response and safety: serial CK and strength testing, swallow reassessment, PFTs, imaging for aspiration/ILD, and surveillance for drug toxicities

sections.section_title: Outcomes, Follow-Up Strategy, and Clinical Pearls
sections.description: Summarizes the patient’s recovery trajectory, outlines ongoing surveillance (including cancer screening), and distills practical lessons to avoid missed dermatomyositis when evaluating unexplained neck swelling.
subtopics: Clinical course: rapid CK normalization, progressive resolution of cervical oedema, recovery of proximal strength, delayed but complete resolution of dysphagia
Long-term plan: tapering immunosuppression (MMF, IVIG), rehabilitation goals, and markers of remission vs relapse

Cancer risk management: applying IMACS risk stratification (dermatomyositis, dysphagia, male sex, SAE1 positivity) and a pragmatic surveillance bundle (exam, labs, serial chest imaging, PET/CT when indicated, and GI endoscopy)
Distinguishing pseudoangioedema from true angioedema in practice: when to obtain CK and examine nailfolds/skin in ‘idiopathic’ facial/neck swelling
Common pitfalls and how to avoid them: absence of classic rashes, anchoring on ENT/allergy diagnoses, overlooking elevated transaminases of muscle origin
Interdisciplinary collaboration: roles for ED, ENT, immunology/rheumatology, neurology, pulmonology, radiology, pathology, and speech therapy in expediting diagnosis and optimizing outcomes
